2.4.2

A bounded harmonic function, which is surely a tempered distribution, must be a polynomial by Corollary 2.4.3, and is a constant as all polynomials tend to ∞ as x→∞.

Suppose that p(z) is a polynomial on C without any complex root. Then the entire function p(z)1​, which is a complex–valued harmonic function on R2, is bounded as it tends to 0 as z→∞, and is therefore a constant by Liouville’s theorem for harmonic functions, yielding a contradiction.

2.4.5

Let w be a smooth function the support of whose Fourier transform is [−1/2,1/2] and let ϕ be a real-valued smooth nonconstant periodic function with period 1, which we can make further assumptions upon later. Then take a family of Schwartz functionsfa​(x)=w(x)eiϕ(x−a)for a∈(0,1/3).Clearly it is an uncountable family of Schwartz functions such that ∣fa​∣=∣fb​∣ for all a and b, and we will show that the fa​’s are linearly independent, which will be addressed later, and that ∣fa​​∣=∣fb​​∣. To this end, we expand the function eiϕ(x) in the Fourier serieseiϕ(x)=k=−∞∑∞​ck​e2πikx.Thenfa​(x)=k=−∞∑∞​ck​e−2πikae2πikxw(x),sofa​​(ξ)=k=−∞∑∞​ck​e−2πikaw(ξ−k).

Since the functions w(ξ−k) are supported in mutually disjoint intervals [k−1/2,k+1/2), we have∣fa​​(ξ)∣=∣ck​w(ξ−k(ξ))∣,where k(ξ) is the integer such that ξ−k(ξ)∈[−1/2,1/2), which shows that ∣fa​​(ξ)∣ is independent of a.

Now we return to the linear independence of the fa​’s, under certain additional assumption on ϕ. Suppose thatk=1∑n​dk​eiϕ(x−ak​)=0for some distinct ak​∈(0,1/3). Let ϕ(x) coincide with x1​ on (1/3,1), thenk=1∑n​dk​ez−ak​i​=0by the uniqueness of meromorphic functions as the left side equals 0 for z∈(2/3,1) (hence z−ak​∈(1/3,1)). Taking z=iε+ak​ where ε→0+ gives dk​=0.

2.4.6

We are going to verify that (Py​∗f)(x) satisfies the mean value property and is continuous on R+n+1​. The two properties together imply that f is harmonic. (Sketch: On any ball consider the difference of such a function and the harmonic function solving the Dirichlet problem where the boundary–value is given by its confinement, which supposedly attains its nonzero maximum or minimum on a closed set, at the farthest point away from the center of the ball of which the mean value property fails.)

First establish the mean value property: for a ball B in R+n+1​ centering at (x0​,y0​),−∫B​(Py​∗f)(x)dxˉ​=−∫B​∫Rn​Py​(x−z)f(z)dzdxˉ=∫Rn​( −∫B​ Py​(x−z)dxˉ)f(z)dz=∫Rn​Py0​​(x0​−z)f(z)dz=(Py0​​∗f)(x0​),​where xˉ=(x,y) and a slash through an integral denotes an average.

Then check its continuity:∣(Py′​∗f)(x′)−(Py​∗f)(x)∣≤∥Py′​(x′−x+⋅)−Py​(⋅)∥Lp′​∥f∥Lp​→0​as (x′,y′)→(x,y), where p1​+p′1​=1 and ∥Py′​(x′−x+⋅)−Py​(⋅)∥Lp′​→0 is easily confirmed by, say, the Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem.

To show that Py1​​∗Py2​​=Py1​+y2​​, it suffices to show that their Fourier transforms agree. Indeed, applying Proposition 2.2.11 (8) and Exercise 2.2.11, Py​​=(y−nδyP)∧=δyP=e−2πy∣ξ∣,so(Py1​​∗Py2​​)∧=Py1​​​Py2​​​=e−2πy1​∣ξ∣e−2πy2​∣ξ∣=e−2π(y1​+y2​)∣ξ∣=Py1​+y2​​​.
